title: Biraj Bhattarai
text: Biraj is interested in understanding cognitive processing in neuro-communication disorder, specifically aphasia. His research utilizes neuroimaging technology like fNIRS to assess neural correlates of cognition, language, and related functions in persons with aphasia. He is a doctoral student at Louisiana State University.

title: Dr. Sajana Aryal
text: Sajana’s research focuses on subclinical auditory damage, particularly the significance of extended high-frequency hearing and its implications for speech perception and neurophysiological processing. She is motivated to understand how early auditory damage influences neural mechanisms and perceptual outcomes, shaping broader implications for hearing health. She is a PhD graduate from the University of Texas at Austin.

title: Kirk Goddard
text: Kirk is an NLP Engineer with an expertise in natural language processing, linguistics, and cognitive neuroscience. He has a blend of experience working across academia and industry. He has studied and researched topics like eye movements in reading (at the University of Massachusetts Amherst) and auditory feedback alteration in speech production (at the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language, BCBL). Following that, he worked on Siri at Apple as a linguist. Currently, he is an NLP Engineer at WRITER working on the application and development of AI and AI-adjacent technologies.

title: Sajana is now Dr. Sajana Aryal
text:

title: About
text:
Nepal Center for Cognition and Society (NCCS) is an independent not-for-profit research organization founded in Bhadrapur, southeastern Nepal. We are a team of researchers distributed globally,  working in interdisciplinary collaboration to study cognitive and related health sciences. At present, NCCS is in a developmental phase. We are initiating pilot research projects, building collaborations with researchers and labs in Nepal and internationally, and establishing access to technical infrastructure through institutional partnerships. 


Why NCCS
A large proportion of research in cognitive and psychological sciences are based on populations from the Western Educated Industrialized Rich and Democratic (WEIRD) societies. In the light of ongoing replication crisis, questions have arose whether such findings are generalizable and are representative of entire humanity. However, the diverse populations of the Global South, including Nepal, is severely under-represented in the cognitive science research. NCCS aims to address this gap by conducting cross-cultural research on the non-WEIRD population answering fundamental questions of human cognition.
This expands the scope of cognitive and brain sciences not just its geography and representation (i.e., predominantly in the western hemisphere with an under-representation of the Global South researchers), but also brings in the possibility of diverse scientific minds in answering the questions of the mind/brain.


What we do
NCCS’s work spans across three main interconnected areas.

1. Research
We initiate and collaborate on research projects in cognitive and psychological sciences and related health sciences with a focus on:
Predictive language processing

Predictive processing in typical and atypical population
Contextual probability and cognitive effort in humans and LLMs

Cognitive health and communication disorders

Neurodevelopmental disorders (autism)
Stroke and language impairment (aphasia, dysarthria)
Executive control in decreased sound tolerance (tinnitus, misophonia, hyperacusis)



2. Collaboration
There is a limited number of scientists working in the area of cognitive and psychological sciences with a constrained infrastructure. Considering this, we collaborate with:

Researchers and labs in universities and research institutes globally
Clinicians and practitioners in health-related fields
Institutions that can provide access to lab facilities and technical resources

Through collaborations, we aim to build methodological capacity and enable cross-cultural research.


3. Science Education and Communication
At NCCS, we believe that science education is foundational to long-term research development. We introduce students to scientific thinking and research methodology, supporting early exposure to cognitive science concepts. We also aim to promote public understanding of how modern scientific knowledge is produced. NCCS also aspires to interact with leaders of different fields to understand and promote diverse local methods of knowledge production, besides modern scientific methods. These activities are intended to contribute to the gradual development of a research culture in Nepal.

title: Nepal Center for Cognition and Society
text:
Our Mission
To contribute to the advancement of cognitive and psychological sciences by generating and supporting research on underrepresented populations, while fostering a culture of scientific inquiry and education in Nepal


Our Vision
We are building NCCS into a globally recognized, independently operating research institute producing globally relevant and locally meaningful scientific knowledge.
Our long-term goal is to demonstrate that rigorous, reproducible cognitive science can be conducted sustainably from a non-WEIRD context, and that geography and early infrastructure constraints are not ceilings on scientific ambition.
We envision NCCS as a center where researchers from across diverse areas of cognitive sciences come together to collaborate and conduct interdisciplinary research. NCCS will become a leading institute housing in-house and remote labs, PIs, and trainees, regularly contributing to the global knowledge base of cognitive science and to the relevant policy-making of the country.
We aim to be a model for research institutions across the Global South working towards similar ambition.


Our Values

Scientific rigor and openness
We are committed to rigorous, open, and reproducible research practice. We pre-register our studies, and make code and data publicly available where applicable. Human subject research is conducted under formal IRB oversight.


Equity and inclusion
We believe there should be no gatekeeping in science, and no discrimination based on one’s caste, gender, or geography. Being mindful of historical inequities, we support efforts to broaden participation in science.


Contextual relevance
We recognize that cognitive processes are shaped by one’s environment and cultural contexts. We prioritize research that seeks to understand cognition through the cross-cultural lens in the non-WEIRD populations, realizing the local and regional contexts.


Collaboration
We view collaboration is essential not only for individual research but for creating and sustaining the research environment broadly, particularly in the resource-constrained setting. We actively seek collaboration with stakeholders of science in Nepal and globally that enable mutual learning, capacity building, and co-create research and policy.


Capacity building
Conducting rigorous research in Nepal takes effort and resources that adapts and lasts beyond a single project. Through our work, we are interested in contributing to gradual development of Nepal’s research infrastructure, capacity, and scientific culture.

title: Research
text:
NCCS supports and develops research in cognitive science and related health science with a focus on underrepresented populations and cross-cultural contexts in Nepal. We also promote such research in similar low- and middle-income settings.
As an organization established in 2025, we are currently in an early-stage research development phase, with a small number of projects active and in preparation.

Ongoing research projects (NCCS-led)
Following projects are being inititated and conducted under NCCS:

Predictive processing in typical and atypical population

Area: Predictive language processing, Developmental stuttering
Status: Under IRB review
Methods: Lab-based behavioral experiment, Computational analysis
PI: Dr. Pratik Bhandari  

Misophonia in Nepali adolescents

Area: Sound sensitivity, Public health
Status: Under IRB review
Methods: Survey-based study
PI: Dr. Sajana Aryal  

Hearing loss in Nepal

Area: Audiology, Public health
Status: Ongoing
Methods: Meta-analysis
PI: Dr. Pratik Bhandari





Prior research by our members
NCCS brings together researchers who are affiliated with universities and institutions around the world. Below is the list of projects that they have undertaken across different institutions prior to and alongside NCCS:

Advancing hearing health research in low- and middle-income countries: Bhandari & Aryal (2026), A. Bhattarai et al. (2024), Raza et al. (2023), Aryal et al. (2022)
Cognitive-communication & neurodegenerative conditions: B. Bhattarai et al. (2021)
Understanding the mechanism behind sound sensitivity disorders: Aryal et al. (2025), Prabhu et al. (2025), Aryal & Prabhu (2024), Aryal & Prabhu (2023)
Aphasia & stroke-related communication disorders: B. Bhattarai & Mohapatra (2026), Mohapatra & Bhattarai (2025), Mohapatra & Bhattarai (2023), B. Bhattarai & Panchakshari (2022)
Executive control in bilinguals: Bhandari et al. (2020), Mishra et al. (2019)
Speech comprehension in adverse listening conditions: Bhandari (2022), Bhandari et al. (2024), Bhandari et al. (2022), Bhandari et al. (2021)
Pediatric & special populations: Fameen et al. (2022), Bhatarai et al. (2020)
Telepractice & technology-based service delivery: Mohapatra & Bhattarai (2023), B. Bhattarai, Sanghavi, & Panchakshari (2022), B. Bhattarai, Sanghavi, & Abhishek (2022)
Psychological response to covid-19 pandemic: Lieberoth et al. (2021)
Neurodiversity: Bhandari & Khanal (2016)




Research approach
Realizing that we are situated in a under-resourced settings, we adapt the following approach in our research:

Utilizing external ethics review (IRB) mechanisms
Engaging in cross-cultural and replication-focused research
Collaborating with external institutions for lab access and research infrastructures
Using scalable and context-appropriate methods, necessatitating fewer resources (behavioral, computational, survey-based)




Open science and tools
We support transparent and reproducible research practices. We:

Share code and tools
Document research workflows
Contribute to open scientific resources

Selected materials and repositories, whenever possible, are shared on our GitHub and OSF repositories.



Collaborate on research
We are actively seeking collaborators for:

Joint research projects
Cross-cultural studies
Student mentorship and training
Grant applications

If your work aligns with our focus areas, please contact us here.

title: Events

Summer 2023: Mentors Retreat at ESIP
The July 17 NASA Openscapes Mentors Retreat will bring together mentors from across seven+ DAACs that have engaged as leaders in the NASA Openscapes project. We see the main value of this retreat as a chance to solidify these cross-DAAC relationships, share lessons learned, problem solve, and ignite new collaborations across the DAACs.
Over the last two years, the mentors have built a community across DAACs, created resources in the Earthdata Cloud Cookbook and supported early adopter users migrating their workflows to the cloud. The goal of the 1-day retreat is to plan the long-term sustainability of the Mentors community from both the governance and technical side.
The NASA Openscapes Mentor Retreat will be in Burlington, Vermont on Monday, July 17 before the ESIP Summer Meeting, July 18-21. We will also provide the opportunity for the Mentors to attend the ESIP Meeting in order to network and learn from the broader community. All registration, travel, accommodation, per diems will be covered.

title: Kranti Acharya
text: Kranti is a clinical researcher interested in cross-cultural issues in the assessment and treatment of cognitive-communication disorders, such as the reliability and validity of tests developed in English languages on the Nepali population. She is an Assistant Professor at the National Academy of Medical Sciences (NAMS), Bir Hospital, Kathmandu.

title: Dr. Pratik Bhandari
text:
Pratik is the founder and Director of Research at NCCS.  He studies how the brain/mind processes sound, speech, and language in typical and atypical populations. His research spans across predictive language processing, developmental language disorders, cognitive consequences of multilingualism, speech perception, among others.
He brings his academic and research experience from across different research institutes and universities from India, Spain, and Germany to Nepal. Focusing on underrepresented, non-WEIRD, diverse communities, he aims to expand the scope of cognitive science in resource-constrained settings like that of Nepal. He is also an Adjunct Faculty Member at the National Academy of Medical Sciences (NAMS), Bir Hospital, Kathmandu.
